item.title: Closing the assurance gap
item.dc:creator: Serj Hallam
item.description:
NIST SP 1800-42A, the OpenID identity proofing extension, and the FinCEN FAQs By Juliana Cafik, Identity Standards & Solutions Architect and independent expert contributing to the OpenID Foundation’s eKYC & IDA Working Group.   On the heels of the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence Phase 1 results, NIST has published draft SP 1800-42A, a practice guide […]

The post Closing the assurance gap first appeared on OpenID Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
On the heels of the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence Phase 1 results, NIST has published draft SP 1800-42A, a practice guide that documents a tested architecture for accepting mobile driver’s licenses when opening a financial account. The OpenID Foundation’s eKYC & IDA Working Group is specifying an identity proofing extension that informs relying parties, such as financial institutions, how a person’s identity was proofed, and to what assurance level, before a credential was issued. On 8 September 2026, FinCEN, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA, and OCC published FAQs confirming that a government-issued verifiable digital credential may qualify as documentary identification under the Customer Identification Program rule.

Read together, they are an implementation path: a reference architecture, a way to express the assurance behind the credential, and a compliance position for using it. None of the three is enough on its own. The architecture does not say how the holder was proofed. The proofing claims do not, by themselves, satisfy the CIP rule. The FAQs do not tell an institution how to verify an issuer, or which protocol to present over.

That is the gap the OpenID Foundation took to the Global Digital Collaboration conference in Geneva, 1–3 September 2026. In the session Closing the Assurance Gap: Securing Financial Account Opening with Verifiable Digital Credentials, OpenID Foundation Liaison Juliana Cafik presented alongside Ryan Galluzzo (NIST), Loffie Jordaan (AAMVA), and Mark Verstege (Austroads). The panel was built around the dependency those three developments expose: credentials have to be issued, proofing rigor has to be expressed, and the result has to map to a financial institution’s regulatory obligations. Remove any one and the chain stops short of meeting financial institution requirements.
